title: Mitigating Reward Hacking in LLM-based Recommendation: A Preference Optimization Approach
claim: Pairwise preference optimization leaves unsampled negatives in insensitive regions, so training reward metrics rise while true ranking quality stalls.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, heatmap and bar charts, then dual-axis plot
description: The figure has three parts. On the left, a red gradient region is labeled the 0.99-insensitive region of the Bradley–Terry model. Two points in it link to small bar charts of item rewards for the initial model and the learned model, with an arrow labeled preference optimization between them. Blue is the positive item, orange the sampled negative and green the unsampled negative. In the learned model the sampled negative drops but the unsampled negative stays high. In the middle, a dashed-outline flow reads Reward Increase, then Inference Wrong with the ranking green > blue > orange, then No Effective Update, with the math p(positive > unsampled) changing little. On the right, a dual-axis plot over epochs 0–5 shows reward-margin bars and Hit Ratio@1 lines. S-DPO's margin rises while its HR@1 stays flat, and the proposed method's HR@1 climbs.

abstract: Post-training adaptation has become the central paradigm for leveraging large language models (LLMs) in recommendation. While recent preference optimization methods, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), enhance pairwise preference discrimination, they remain vulnerable to \emph{reward hacking}: models exploit imperfections in reward signals, leading to inflated training metrics without genuine recommendation gains. We analyze this issue from a gradient perspective and formalize the concept of the \emph{$\varepsilon$-insensitive region}, where pairwise updates exert little influence on the ordering between positives and unsampled negatives. Under the Bradley–Terry model, we further show that these regions can occupy a substantial fraction of the preference space, inevitably leading to misaligned rankings. To address this issue, we propose Simulated Preference Optimization for Reward-hacking mitigation using Pseudo-negatives (SIRIUS). Our framework introduces pseudo-negative samples to enrich contrastive signals and reduce the prevalence of $\varepsilon$-insensitive regions. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks show that \our{} consistently improves ranking quality and effectively mitigates reward hacking, providing both theoretical and practical insights for advancing LLM-based recommendation. Our code is available at \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/C557-id}
